awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Percutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Paddle Lead Using Shape Memory Polymer
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is a minimally invasive novel spinal cord stimulation (SCS) lead and procedure for use with spinal cord stimulators to treat chronic pain. Chronic back pain is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide affecting over 50 million adults in the US. Implantable SCS systems have been previously demonstrated to mitigate chronic back pain with an estimated $2.1 billion market.   The novel approach combines the benefits of the two currently available types of spinal cord leads: cylindrical percutaneous and surgical paddle. Paddle leads offer greater coverage, better energy efficiency, and lower migration risk over cylindrical percutaneous leads but require more invasive surgical procedures to place. This project will develop a flexible multielectrode interface to improve therapeutic coverage and efficiency that enables minimally invasive placement through a needle. If successful, the project will reduce the invasiveness of current lead placement procedures, improve the rate of successful procedures, reduce opioid usage associated with back pain treatment, and reduce the estimated $300 billion in annual healthcare costs associated with chronic back pain in the US. 
 
This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will develop a novel minimally invasive procedure deploying an implantable Spinal Cord Stimulation (SCS) lead by utilizing a shape memory polymer (SMP). Current SCS placement procedures require surgical interventions with high rates of chronic morbidity and adverse events.  This project develops an 8-channel SMP-based paddle lead that can be molded into a compact configuration for transport and bodily introduction through a tuohy needle, thereby reducing the surgical implications. Once placed, the lead re-expands to provide the benefits of a traditional paddle lead. Finite element computer simulations will determine the best shape to mold the paddle into for transport and successful deployment. Paddle leads will be fabricated using microfabrication processes in accordance with medical device practices, characterized, and tested using benchtop models of the spine. Upon completion the project will demonstrate the feasibility of a novel minimally invasive SCS paddle lead placement procedural system for use with spinal cord stimulators to mitigate chronic back pain.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established treatment that delivers electrical pulses through implanted electrodes to help manage chronic pain which affects tens of millions of Americans and is a major cause of disability worldwide. There also is emerging research showing that SCS can be an effective therapy for other conditions including movement recovery after spinal cord injury or stroke. Current devices use two main types of leads: cylindrical leads are inserted through an epidural needle in a minimally invasive procedure but provide limited coverage and may move after implantation; wider paddle leads offer greater coverage and stability but are thicker and require surgery for placement.

With support from the National Science Foundation's Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, Backstop Neural, Inc. investigated whether the advantages of both approaches could be combined. The project explored the development of a novel SCS paddle lead featuring electrodes microfabricated on a shape memory polymer (SMP), a material that can be deformed into a temporary shape and recover its original shape when exposed to a stimulus such as heat or moisture.

Project activities. The team characterized how the polymer's stiffness and shape recovery changed with temperature, hydration, and material composition. Developed computer models then predicted mechanical stresses and strains with deformation and deployment behavior. Four rolled or bent paddle lead configurations were evaluated for delivery through a standard epidural needle using simulations and benchtop experiments. The team also fabricated electrode samples with thin-film gold conductors and titanium nitride electrodes to assess electrochemical properties when flat, bent into transport configurations, and once deployed. Two custom testing systems were built to carry out the project goals: an imaging system to track shape recovery in real time, and a high-current biphasic stimulator to directly measure electrode charge injection capacity using voltage transients.

Key findings. The project demonstrated the strong electrical performance of novel fabricated electrodes on SMP and identified important design rules for future implantable electrodes. All tested electrode designs met the project's charge delivery requirements, including post bending and deployment. Their charge storage capacity substantially exceeded the target value, and titanium nitride electrodes demonstrated several times the charge delivery capability of similarly sized conventional platinum-iridium electrodes. The results also established a relationship between electrode surface area and charge injection, guiding reduced electrode size while maintaining clinically relevant stimulation levels. Mechanical testing revealed another important design principle: continuous metal films can wrinkle during tight bending whereas appropriately segmented films better withstand the same deformation.

The project also established a fundamental limitation of the proposed needle delivery approach. Among four configurations, only the simplest rolled design exceeded 90% deployment and only when heated substantially above body temperature. At body temperature, none recovered to the intended deployment. Experiments and simulations showed that as the polymer underwent shape recovery, it became too soft to generate the mechanical force needed for complete deployment under these conditions. Consequently, needle-based deployment using the SMP’s recovery mechanism was not feasible with the tested material properties and device dimensions.

Although needle delivery of the SMP-based leads was infeasible with the proposed constraints, simulations and testing showed bending a paddle lead to conform to the spinal cord did not negatively affect mechanical or electrical performance; a shape change was more practical for the supported commercial application. NSF I-Corps customer discovery activities validated commercialization of Backstop Neural’s SCS lead in movement recovery applications for spinal cord injury patients, and interviews with clinicians and key stakeholders revealed close, stable contact with the spinal cord was more important than minimally invasive delivery.

Intellectual merit. The project developed and experimentally informed mechanical models describing the behavior of SMPs in microfabricated implantable devices. These models established quantitative relationships among material stiffness, temperature, device geometry, mechanical deformation, and shape recovery. Combined with the electrode characterization and fabrication results, the research generated practical design rules for improving the flexibility, electrical performance, and reliability of future neural interfaces.

Broader impacts. The validated polymer platform, wafer-scale fabrication methods, and electrode design principles have potential applications beyond SCS, including other thin, conformal bioelectronic implants. These advances contribute to the development of manufacturing technologies for next-generation medical devices. Through NSF-supported customer discovery activities, the team completed more than 100 interviews with clinicians, rehabilitation specialists, spinal cord injury patients, manufacturers, and other stakeholders, and these discussions identified unmet clinical needs guiding future development priorities. The project additionally strengthened collaborations with UT Dallas, providing research and training opportunities for an undergraduate student.

Next steps. Building on the demonstrated feasibility of Backstop Neural’s technologies, the company will advance development of a surgically implanted, conformal cervical SCS lead designed to support upper limb movement recovery after spinal cord injury. The Phase I results provide the technical foundation and design guidance for this next stage of testing and validation ahead of commercialization.
